item.title: Italie-Les boutiques de Milan ont fermé plus tôt, craintes de nouveaux pillages
item.description: Les magasins du centre de Milan ont fermé plus tôt que d'habitude lundi et ont barricadé leurs vitrines, craignant de nouveaux troubles après deux jours de manifestations au cours desquels des groupes de personnes cagoulées se sont affrontés avec la police, ont pillé des magasins et saccagé des biens.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Les magasins du centre de Milan ont fermé plus tôt que d'habitude lundi et ont barricadé leurs vitrines, craignant de nouveaux troubles après deux jours de manifestations au cours desquels des groupes de personnes cagoulées se sont affrontés avec la police, ont pillé des magasins et saccagé des biens. La plupart des boutiques de luxe de la Via Montenapoleone, où sont implantées des marques telles que Chanel, Tiffany et Dior, ont retiré leurs articles de vitrine par mesure de précaution. La police italienne a interpellé 271 individus lors des troubles survenus dimanche à Milan, ont déclaré lundi les autorités, après des violences en marge d'une deuxième journée de manifestations contre la dégradation des services publics et la hausse du coût de la vie. Des enseignes de sport telles que Decathlon et Arc'teryx ou encore celle de téléphonie Vodafone ont été pillées, au cours de ces vioolences, selon des images diffusées à la télévision. Parmi les personnes emmenées au poste de police, trente-deux ont été placées en garde à vue, dont vingt-trois mineurs et treize ressortissants étrangers. Vingt-huit autres individus ont été déférés devant les autorités judiciaires. Ces incidents font suite à des affrontements similaires survenus samedi dans des villes du nord, notamment Bologne, Brescia, Bergame et Turin, où vingt-huit manifestants ont été arrêtés, selon la police. La présidente du Conseil Giorgia Meloni, dont la coalition de droite est, selon les sondages, loin d'être donnée favorite pour les élections nationales de 2027, a condamné ces violences et a présidé lundi une réunion avec ses ministres et les responsables de la sécurité afin d’examiner la situation. Le gouvernement prévoit d’adopter des mesures proposées par la police visant à prévenir et à lutter contre de telles flambées de violence, a déclaré une source gouvernementale, ajoutant que ces propositions seraient soumises lors d’une réunion du Conseil des ministres prévue mardi. Selon le Corriere della Sera, Giorgia Meloni envisage ainsi de rallonger la détention préventive pour les mineurs et de sévir contre les gangs de jeunes.

item.title: Saudi Arabia postpones its 'Davos in the Desert' conference after attacks
item.description: Saudi Arabia has decided to postpone its flagship investment conference until next year, organizers confirmed in a statement on Monday, following deadly attacks which rocked the kingdom in recent weeks as the Middle East conflict widens, disrupting business.
item.dc:creator: Timour Azhari, Federico Maccioni, Tala Ramadan, Alexander Cornwell
item.content:encoded: Saudi Arabia has decided to postpone its flagship investment [USN:L6N4600CJ TEXT:"conference"] until next year, organizers confirmed in a statement on Monday, following deadly attacks which rocked the kingdom in recent weeks as the Middle East conflict widens, disrupting business. The Future Investment Initiative, or FII, was planned for October 26 to 29, but will now take place in 2027, with a new date to be announced "very soon," the organizers said. Reuters [USN:L6N4650WL TEXT:"reported"] earlier Monday that the in-person event had been scrapped and organizers were weighing postponing the event. The conference, set for its 10th edition, has become a must-attend event for some of the world's top financiers. Informally dubbed "Davos in the Desert," in a nod to the World Economic Forum's annual meeting in Switzerland, the state-backed annual event has showcased the kingdom's ambitious investment plans in a bid to attract billions of dollars needed to fund its economic transformation away from hydrocarbons towards tourism, sports and technology. Expected speakers for this year's event included Goldman Sachs (GS.N) CEO and Chairman David Solomon, Standard Chartered (STAN.L) CEO Bill Winters and Citi's CEO Jane Fraser, according to a draft programme. The US-Israeli war with Iran this year has disrupted the Gulf's busy calendar of events, with several conferences cancelled, postponed or retooled in the UAE and Qatar in the first part of the year, when the countries bore the brunt of the attacks while Saudi Arabia suffered [USN:L6N42B0X9 TEXT:"fewer"] hits. The kingdom in recent weeks has faced an escalating war with Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis, which have [USN:L6N4600NM TEXT:"struck"] military, energy and civilian infrastructure across the country, including state oil company Aramco's headquarters and Riyadh's international airport, where strikes [USN:L8N45X021 TEXT:"killed"] at least 18 people and hundreds were wounded this month. FII said it wanted to ensure the event delivered "the full scale, extraordinary quality, and unforgettable impact that our community has come to expect." Reuters reported last week that the FII organizers considered a hybrid format, allowing executives to tune in remotely. Semafor reported Monday that big banks and private-equity firms have privately relayed safety concerns about attending the event to Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund Governor Yasir Al-Rumayyan, adding that CEOs feel pressure to attend the four-day event.

item.title: Eyes in the skies: How satellites are boosting confidence in forest carbon projects
item.description: Once every three days, as the European Space Agency’s Biomass satellite races across the sky at a speed of 27,000 kilometres per hour, it passes over a specific point within the Congo rainforest, the mighty expanse of greenery in the heart of Africa. As it completes this circuit, the satellite beams data back to Earth, allowing scientists to piece together a 3D scan to monitor the health of the forest.
item.dc:creator: Ben Payton
item.content:encoded: Once every three days, as the European Space Agency’s Biomass satellite races across the sky at a speed of 27,000 kilometres per hour, it passes over a specific point within the Congo rainforest, the mighty expanse of greenery in the heart of Africa. As it completes this circuit, the satellite beams data back to Earth, allowing scientists to piece together a 3D scan to monitor the health of the forest. Biomass, launched from French Guiana in April 2025, is one of a growing number of satellites tasked with surveying the Earth’s forests. Uniquely, it uses P-band synthetic aperture radar (SAR). By transmitting ultra-long radio waves that penetrate the forest canopy, the satellite can measure tree trunks and branches, which provides a proxy for the amount of carbon being stored. Satellites like Biomass are “absolutely essential” for rainforest conservation, says Donna Lyndsay, climate services development manager at Space4Climate, a public-private partnership that promotes the use of satellite data for climate action. She notes that cutting-edge satellites are now orbiting the Earth at a greater cadence, providing increasingly high-resolution spatial imagery that can offer early warning signs of any deterioration in forest health. As the pace of climate change escalates, monitoring threats to tropical forests – and, ultimately, intervening to counter these threats – has never been so important. L-band SAR, a less advanced technology than P-band, has been key to helping scientists realise that Africa’s forests and woody savannahs have already passed a tipping point. According to findings published in the journal Scientific Reports , rapid deforestation means these African biomes have been releasing more carbon than they sequester since 2010. Logs lie next to a rusting barge on the banks of the Congo river. REUTERS/David Lewis Alongside continuous innovation in the hardware of satellites, breakthroughs on the software side are enabling scientists to make ever-greater use of satellite data. “We have now, through the use of AI capabilities, the ability to really interrogate these datasets on a massive scale,” says Lyndsay. This is paving the way for a significant expansion in predictive analytics, she says. A company might, for example, receive an alert that signals of impending deforestation have been detected within areas from which its sources commodities. Armed with this data, the company could then consider taking preventative action. The Congo rainforest stretches across Cameroon, the Central African Republic, Congo-Brazzaville, Equatorial Guinea and Gabon, as well as DR Congo itself. With much of its expanse virtually inaccessible by road, Satellites offer the only practical way of keeping track of deforestation threats. “I don't think there's any way that we could possibly have oversight of all natural forests globally, without having some sort of bird’s-eye view of what's going on,” says Lucy Barnes, a senior manager for supply chain solutions at the Earthworm Foundation. The non-profit has been running a satellite monitoring platform called Starling with Airbus since 2016 that can alert major companies to risks of deforestation in their supply chains. Improved technology will open new possibilities for using satellite data, Barnes adds. “It's not necessarily about using it just for monitoring deforestation, as such. I think in some ways, we’re able to do that to a very high level now. It's how you can also use that data for answering other environmental questions, for example, measuring carbon sequestration.” Indeed, multiple actors in the carbon markets space are already making extensive use of satellite data. The hope is that satellite data could even help solve some of the longstanding problems that have undermined the growth of these markets. REDD+ carbon credit schemes have been heavily promoted as a way to avoid emissions linked to deforestation, yet these schemes have repeatedly been criticised for alleged “over-crediting”. An image of Sumatra in western Indonesia via Starling, a satellite monitoring platform run by Earthworm Foundation and Airbus. Starling/Handout via REUTERS In a notorious example, project developer Carbon Green Investments and environmental consultancy South Pole grossly overstated the rate of deforestation in a “reference area” close to the forest they were seeking to preserve through the Kariba REDD+ project in Zimbabwe. This allowed the developer to claim its interventions within the project area made a greater impact in avoiding emissions than was truly the case. Following a lengthy investigation, carbon markets registry Verra found last year that the project had issued more than twice as many credits as it should have done. In the wake of these reputational disasters, the price of avoided deforestation credits remains depressed. Even higher-rated REDD+ credits trade at only around $7 per tonne, according to data from carbon markets intelligence firm Sylvera. By comparison, high-rated projects that remove carbon through reforestation or afforestation average $26.10 per tonne. Yet experts agree that there is no higher priority for climate and biodiversity than protecting existing forest habitats. In other words, there is a misalignment in the market between the financial value of afforestation versus the conservation value of avoiding deforestation in the first place. Satellite monitoring could help solve this conundrum. Phil Platts, senior vice president for geospatial and Earth observation at carbon ratings agency BeZero Carbon, notes that newer avoided deforestation methodologies – such as Verra’s VM0048 – take responsibility for determining the baseline used to calculate deforestation rates away from project developers. Instead, registries use satellite imagery to calculate deforestation rates across a country or province; credit issuance is then based on comparing deforestation in the project area with the wider jurisdiction. The “systematic over-crediting” that once marred avoided deforestation projects “just isn’t there with these new methodologies,” Platts says. Finland-based ICEYE is partnering with the Jane Goodall Foundation to support chimpanzee conservation in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo by using SAR to detect logging and illegal mining. REUTERS/James Akena Despite these advances, the carbon markets remain controversial. Rainforest Foundation UK’s executive director Joe Eisen describes the market as a “folly” in the forests of central Africa, warning that revenues are “not filtering down to communities where it's most needed”. Nevertheless, Rainforest Foundation UK is working on a pilot project in 30 community forests in the Democratic Republic of Congo, in which communities receive payments based on protecting forest cover. The verification of results is “based entirely on satellite data”, Eisen says. The NGO also operates a satellite monitoring platform called ForestEye, which can provide community forest monitoring groups with access to intelligence on disturbance to the forest canopy. As both hardware and software continues to improve, satellite technology will play an increasingly key role both in monitoring forest carbon projects, and in supporting rainforest conservation more generally. One company pushing the boundaries of what satellite monitoring can do is ICEYE, a Finland-headquartered company that operates the world’s largest constellation of SAR satellites. In April, it announced a partnership with the Jane Goodall Foundation to support chimpanzee conservation in eastern DRC by using SAR to detect threats such as logging and illegal mining. Michael Bennett, ICEYE’s head of government solutions, says conventional satellite monitoring is insufficient in this region, which is blanketed by thick clouds for much of the year. Illegal activities can easily remain undetected beneath the thick forest canopy. DRC has been losing roughly 0.5% of its primary forests each year over the past decade, largely due to encroachment of small-scale agriculture. REUTERS/Arlette Bashizi “With SAR, you don't need to get lucky,” he says. Much like the ESA’s Biomass satellite, the radar beams transmitted by ICEYE’s satellites can penetrate both cloud and canopy cover to build a 3D image that make it easier to detect possible threats. And while conservation organisations might traditionally rely on satellite images that are several months, or even years, out of date, Bennett stresses that ICEYE’s constellation of dozens of satellites in low Earth orbit mean the company can provide “near-real time” coverage. Of course, gaining these kinds of insights is only the first step. There is still the problem of how to intervene in an environment where the government’s authority is limited at best. With a more accurate picture of threats to chimpanzees, however, Bennett suggests the Jane Goodall Foundation will be able to become more proactive in alerting authorities and on-the-ground team to the need for action. Sassan Saatchi is CEO of CTrees, a platform that offers free access to data on carbon sequestration down to the level of an individual tree. While hailing the advances in satellite technology, he says more work is needed to ensure that increasingly abundant sources of data are actually used by local teams, both in carbon projects and in broader conservation efforts. “There is so much free material and technology they can use,” he says. “If they use it, it would be a significant change.” The dangers facing the great forests of central Africa and their wealth of biodiversity remain formidable. DRC has been losing roughly 0.5% of its primary forests each year over the past decade, largely due to encroachment of small-scale agriculture. And Cameroon suffered its worst ever year of deforestation in 2025, partly driven by the growth of cocoa plantations. Thanks to satellite data, governments, NGOs and companies have a clearer picture than ever before on the health of Africa’s forests. The challenge now, with the help of satellite tools, is to find ways to ensure these green lungs can survive forever. item.title: Neue Regierung Ungarns plant deutliche Senkung des Haushaltsdefizits
item.description: Ungarn strebt für das kommende Jahr eine deutliche Senkung seines Haushaltsdefizits auf 4,9 Prozent des Bruttoinlandsprodukts (BIP) an. Den entsprechenden Haushaltsentwurf stellte Ministerpräsident Peter Magyar am Montag vor. Das Vorhaben gilt als wichtiger Prüfstein für die Glaubwürdigkeit des Ziels, den Euro einzuführen. Die geplante Verringerung wäre ein deutlicher Rückgang gegenüber dem für dieses Jahr erwarteten Defizit von 7,5 Prozent. Zudem ist das Ziel ehrgeiziger als die von Analysten in einer Reuters-Umfrage prognostizierten 5,3 Prozent.

item.content:encoded: Ungarn strebt für das kommende Jahr eine deutliche Senkung seines Haushaltsdefizits auf 4,9 Prozent des Bruttoinlandsprodukts (BIP) an. Den entsprechenden Haushaltsentwurf stellte Ministerpräsident Peter Magyar am Montag vor. Das Vorhaben gilt als wichtiger Prüfstein für die Glaubwürdigkeit des Ziels, den Euro einzuführen. Die geplante Verringerung wäre ein deutlicher Rückgang gegenüber dem für dieses Jahr erwarteten Defizit von 7,5 Prozent. Zudem ist das Ziel ehrgeiziger als die von Analysten in einer Reuters-Umfrage prognostizierten 5,3 Prozent. Magyar versucht, das Defizit mittelfristig unter die EU-Obergrenze von drei Prozent - eines der Euro-Kriterien - zu drücken, ohne dabei seine Wahlversprechen zu brechen. Er hatte im April einen Erdrutschsieg über Viktor Orban errungen. Die geplanten Mehrausgaben sollen im kommenden Jahr mehr als zwei Billionen Forint (rund 5,7 Milliarden Euro) betragen. Gleichzeitig will die Regierung Einsparungen von 1,5 Billionen Forint (rund 3,8 Milliarden Euro) vornehmen. Die Einnahmen sollen durch eine neue Vermögenssteuer, eine höhere Körperschaftssteuer für Großkonzerne sowie höhere Steuern für Energieunternehmen gesteigert werden. Der Entwurf sieht zudem Steuersenkungen für mehr als zwei Millionen Steuerzahler im Umfang von 250 Milliarden Forint (rund 625 Millionen Euro) vor. Der Einkommensteuersatz auf den Mindestlohn soll auf neun Prozent sinken. Das Ziel der Euro-Einführung hatte zuletzt zu einer Aufwertung des ungarischen Forint beigetragen, was die Inflation unter das Inflationsziel der Zentralbank drückte. Die Renditen für Staatsanleihen fielen auf einen der niedrigsten Werte in Mitteleuropa. Am Montag legte der Forint gegenüber anderen Währungen der Region zu und erreichte den höchsten Stand seit vier Wochen. Analysten rechnen mit einem Beitritt Ungarns zur Eurozone in den Jahren 2032 oder 2033.

item.title: Energy Watch: Elections angst
item.description: Elections are always delicate moments. With Israel's parliamentary vote eight days away and the US midterms following a week later, oil markets are nervously watching the Middle East. Reported Iranian attacks on ships around the Strait of Hormuz reached a record 12 last week, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Elections are always delicate moments. With [USN:FWN4630MG TEXT:"Israel's parliamentary vote"] eight days away and the [USN:L1N4600TJ TEXT:"US midterms"] following a week later, oil markets are nervously watching the Middle East. Reported [USN:S8N45501B TEXT:"Iranian attacks"] on ships around the Strait of Hormuz reached a record 12 last week, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency. What was most telling was not the number itself but the fact that UKMTO admitted that it is struggling to keep count of strikes, "with the majority of vessels attacked refusing to report." This surge in attacks appears to be having a significant impact on flows. Oil exports through the narrow waterway have fallen from a peak of 17 million barrels per day in early October to around 11 million bpd in recent days, Kpler data showed. Yet producers and shippers are still sailing through Hormuz, showing how quickly the industry has adapted to a new normal characterized by severely heightened risk. That resilience comes at a cost, however. Just ask Asian refiners. They purchase the majority of the Middle East's oil, and soaring shipping costs are crushing their profit margins. For more on that, [USN:L6N4620UK TEXT:"check out my latest column"]. Oil prices, meanwhile, hit a 5-month high of over $109 a barrel on Friday, reflecting growing angst among investors that the Iran war could reignite, with President Donald Trump saying the US might [USN:L6N4620Q7 TEXT:"renew strikes"] on Iran's nuclear facilities. Benchmark Brent oil prices slipped on Monday, however. In other news: China's economy [USN:L1N46501H TEXT:"bounced back"] from a three-year low, growing 4.5% in the third quarter and beating forecasts as roaring exports offset consumers' tight grip on their wallets. The strong reading is another sign that the world's top oil importer has largely shielded itself from the worst effects of the Iran war. Chinese oil refineries raised processing rates slightly in September for a third straight month as strong fuel exports supported demand. The world's biggest oil buyer cut crude imports by 21.5% from a year earlier while boosting domestic production. Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney is betting that a new pipeline can revive the country's oil industry, lift production and exports, and reduce the country’s dependence on the United States. Bringing back jobs will be much harder, writes Reuters correspondent Amanda Stephenson. The US and Israeli war against Iran has dominated the energy story in 2026. But the quiet retooling of power grids from Lagos to Manila may prove [USN:L1N45Z15T TEXT:"more significant"] in the long run, writes ROI Energy Transition Columnist Gavin Maguire.
