item.title: El oro cae levemente lastrado por fortaleza del dólar y altos rendimientos
item.description: Los precios del oro cayeron levemente el lunes, presionados por la fortaleza del dólar y el aumento de los rendimientos de los bonos del Tesoro de Estados Unidos, mientras los inversores esperaban la decisión de política monetaria de la Reserva Federal la próxima semana, en la que se prevé que el banco central mantenga las tasas de interés sin cambios.
item.dc:creator: Anushree Mukherjee, Vishak Mathew
item.content:encoded: Los precios del oro cayeron levemente el lunes, presionados por la fortaleza del dólar y el aumento de los rendimientos de los bonos del Tesoro de Estados Unidos, mientras los inversores esperaban la decisión de política monetaria de la Reserva Federal la próxima semana, en la que se prevé que el banco central mantenga las tasas de interés sin cambios. * El oro al contado caía un 0,5%, a 4.143,91 dólares por onza, a las 1534 GMT. Los futuros del oro en Estados Unidos con vencimiento en diciembre cedían un 0,4%, a 4.163,30 dólares por onza. * El dólar estadounidense subía levemente, lo que encarecía el oro denominado en dólares para los tenedores de otras divisas, y los rendimientos de los bonos del Tesoro estadounidense a 10 años subían un 0,6%. * "Existe la preocupación de que los bancos centrales tengan que endurecer aún más sus políticas para controlar la inflación, lo que está dando un nuevo impulso a los rendimientos. Y, dado que los rendimientos se mantienen elevados, los inversores en oro se preguntan si tiene más sentido estar en el mercado de bonos en este momento", dijo Fawad Razaqzada, analista de mercado de Forex.com. * La Fed subió las tasas de interés un cuarto de punto en septiembre, su primera alza de este año. * "No se trata solo de si la Fed subirá las tasas la semana que viene o esperará hasta diciembre; el tono de sus orientaciones será determinante. Un mensaje de línea dura podría provocar una mayor debilidad a corto plazo del oro", añadió Razaqzada. * Según la herramienta FedWatch de la CME, los operadores estiman que hay un 82,8% de probabilidades de que la Fed mantenga las tasas sin cambios este mes, mientras que las expectativas de una subida en diciembre se mantienen en el 90%. * Aunque el oro suele considerarse una cobertura frente a la inflación, el aumento de las tasas de interés reduce el atractivo de este activo, que no rinde intereses. * Los inversores también esperan los datos sobre el gasto en consumo personal de Estados Unidos de la próxima semana, el indicador de inflación preferido por el banco central. * En tanto, los precios del petróleo retrocedían desde su máximo de cinco meses después de que el presidente de Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, suspendió las sanciones y los aranceles a Rusia, lo que podría dar lugar a un aumento de las exportaciones de combustible ruso. * Entre otros metales preciosos, la plata al contado subió un 0,4% a 57,24 dólares por onza, el platino ganó un 1% a 1.646 dólares por onza y el paladio sumó un 0,8% a 1.121,14 dólares por onza.

item.title: China's Hansoh Pharma strikes drug deal with Roche worth over $15 billion
item.description: China's Hansoh Pharmaceutical said on Monday it has entered into a partnership and licensing deal with Roche potentially worth more than $15 billion that covers a portfolio of antibody-drug conjugate programs.
item.dc:creator: Nichiket Sunil, Patrick Wingrove
item.content:encoded: China's Hansoh Pharmaceutical (3692.HK) said on Monday it has entered into a partnership and licensing deal with Roche (ROPC.S) potentially worth more than $15 billion that covers a portfolio of antibody-drug conjugate programs. As part of the deal with the Swiss drugmaker's unit F. Hoffmann-La Roche, Hansoh will receive an upfront payment of $400 million, a first anniversary payment of $110 million and further milestone payments. Antibody-drug conjugates are targeted cancer therapies that act like guided missiles, attaching toxic chemotherapy directly to tumor cells while sparing healthy tissue. Roche currently sells two approved ADCs, Kadcyla and Polivy, that analysts expect to generate a combined 3.5 billion Swiss francs ($4.3 billion) this year, according to LSEG data. Under the terms of the Hansoh partnership, the Chinese company will lead early development until global Phase Ia clinical trials are complete. Roche will then take over worldwide development and commercialization, the Chinese company said, excluding mainland China, Hong Kong, Macau, and Taiwan, where Hansoh retains rights. Hansoh also has the option to take part in developing up to two programs outside those markets. Roche said the collaboration, combined with its own research, gave the company the opportunity to advance antibody-drug conjugates as a central component of its next-generation oncology strategy. The two companies have previously [USN:L6N3VX19N TEXT:"partnered"] on colorectal cancer treatments. ROCHE STEPPING UP DEALMAKING Facing impending patent cliffs on aging blockbusters, Roche is increasingly turning to external dealmaking to rebuild its pipeline and capture next-generation therapies. In August, the Swiss drugmaker's Genentech struck a deal with DualityBio worth up to $1 billion for its ADC therapies. Earlier this month, Roche secured an obesity drug licensing agreement worth up to $1.16 billion with China's Rona Therapeutics, following a January commitment of $100 million upfront for a non-exclusive patent license from Structure Therapeutics covering oral weight-loss drugs. Teaming up with Hansoh could also fast-track Roche’s route to market. While Roche is advancing oral SERDs like giredestrant in breast cancer, its broader late-stage pipeline faces a notable valley until the end of the decade, making external partnerships essential for near-term momentum. Drugmakers have struck over a dozen licensing deals with Chinese companies in the past year, highlighted by AstraZeneca’s $18.5 billion [USN:L4N3YV05G TEXT:"obesity drug pact"] with CSPC in January and Bristol Myers Squibb’s $15.2 billion [USN:L4N41P0BH TEXT:"multi-program alliance"] with China’s top drugmaker, Jiangsu Hengrui, in May.

item.title: Governments warn citizens over security in France after riots
item.description: Governments in Europe and Asia, including China, on Monday advised citizens travelling to France to avoid large crowds and exercise caution, warning of a deterioration in security conditions after thousands were arrested and shops looted in protests over the weekend.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Governments in Europe and Asia, including China, on Monday advised citizens travelling to France to avoid large crowds and exercise caution, warning of a [USN:L6N4650BY TEXT:"deterioration in security conditions"] after thousands were arrested and shops looted in protests over the weekend. Demonstrations across France over high prices and declining public services [USN:L1N46401W TEXT:"erupted into riots"] on Saturday, with a town hall torched as violent groups clashed with police. In response, the foreign ministries of several European countries issued fresh travel warnings. ITALY Italy said its citizens should register their presence in France on a website or an app to enable them to be located, as it warned them to avoid large crowds and exercise extreme caution. GERMANY The German foreign ministry said further riots in the coming days couldn't be ruled out and urged German nationals to follow instructions from local police. It warned citizens that they could face fines or claims for damages if they failed to leave unauthorised demonstrations when asked to do so. CZECH REPUBLIC Czechs in France are advised to avoid demonstrations, marches and public gatherings, CTK news agency reported. The security situation in France has deteriorated, according to the Czech foreign affairs ministry. POLAND Poland said in its country guidance that visitors should avoid places where demonstrations are taking place, though there was no change to its overall guidance about whether France was safe to visit. NETHERLANDS The Dutch government in an advisory last updated on October 7 warned travelers to France to avoid protests. NORDICS Denmark, Sweden, Finland and Norway have issued advisories urging their citizens in France to avoid demonstrations and follow the guidance of local authorities. CHINA China's Foreign Ministry and diplomatic missions in France have urged Chinese nationals planning to travel to the country to remain alert to potential risks, strengthen safety precautions, and avoid areas where demonstrations are taking place, according to state media. MALAYSIA Malaysia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said it is monitoring the demonstrations and that while travel to France remains unrestricted, Malaysians are advised to consider postponing non-essential trips until the situation improves. It said its embassy in Paris has issued an advisory urging Malaysians in France to exercise caution and remain vigilant.

item.title: Alberta votes on leaving Canada; separatist movement likely to outlast expected defeat
item.description: Oil-rich Alberta holds a nonbinding referendum on Monday on whether the western province should secede from Canada, a debate many believe will not be settled by what is widely expected to be a defeat for the separatist cause.
item.dc:creator: Amanda Stephenson
item.content:encoded: Oil-rich Alberta holds a [USN:L6N46019J TEXT:"nonbinding referendum"] on Monday on whether the western province should secede from Canada, a debate many believe will not be settled by what is widely expected to be a defeat for the separatist cause. Polls have consistently shown that a majority of Alberta voters oppose splitting from Canada. Economic grievances have fueled the independence campaign in the province, which is home to 5 million people and slightly smaller than Texas despite having one-sixth the population. The Alberta separatist movement adds to the pressures on Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who has made defending Canada's sovereignty a central mission as he confronts US tariffs and President Donald Trump's repeated calls for Canada to become the 51st state. Many Alberta separatists believe the Liberal Party-led federal government in Ottawa has constrained the Conservative-governed province's oil industry through environmental policies, and that Alberta, the country's energy heartland, contributes more to Canada's economy than it receives in return. "Canada has an imbalanced system which feeds the central population and government at the expense of the outlying producing provinces such as Alberta," said Cory Morgan, founder of a pro-separation advertising organization called Pathway to Independence. Carney, who grew up in Alberta, spent much of the past week campaigning for the "stay" side, urging supporters to vote and appealing to national pride. Polls are scheduled to close at 8 p.m. MDT on Monday (0200 GMT on Tuesday) with results published as they arrive. An Angus Reid poll released Friday showed 66% of Albertans plan to vote to remain in Canada, but three in five believe "there will never be an end to the separatist movement" in the province. "This issue is not going away now. Because the separatists are mobilized. They've networked. They're connected," said Mount Royal University political scientist Duane Bratt in Calgary. While separatist sentiment has existed in the province for decades, Premier Danielle Smith is the first Alberta leader to put the question to voters. Smith, who has urged Albertans to remain in Canada, [USN:L6N41X1E1 TEXT:"called the referendum"] after [USN:L6N3Z2101 TEXT:"months of pressure"] from a small but vocal flank of her governing United Conservative Party. If a majority votes in favor, Smith has said she would seek a binding referendum on separation. "Separating, to my point of view, is completely ridiculous," said Ross Watson of Calgary after casting his ballot in favor of "remain" in an advance poll last week. "I think the grievances that people have are completely unfounded. But I also think these people will probably never shut up." SENDING A MESSAGE Monday's referendum is the first time a vote on separation from the rest of Canada has been held in a province outside majority French-speaking Quebec, where separatist sentiment derives from language and cultural differences. In Alberta, the issue is more about dollars than identity. Carney has appealed to national pride in arguing Alberta should remain part of Canada. "Canada is not a transaction between provinces. It's not about gross and net, gives and gets," Carney said Friday in Red Deer, Alberta. Partly to address the grievances that have driven separatist sentiment in Alberta, Carney has [USN:L1N3X30IC TEXT:"overturned "]some environmental policies and supported a proposed [USN:L1N45N0PP TEXT:"oil pipeline "]that would increase Alberta's exports to Asia. Among the one-third of Albertans who would vote in favor of a future binding referendum on separation, 60% told pollsters their motivation was to "send a message" to Canada's federal government. Only 37% of respondents to the Angus Reid poll said their motivation was an independent nation. Separatist groups have published transition plans, but key questions about how independence would work on issues such as defence, currency and border controls remain unresolved. Bratt said the real question is where the movement goes from here. "Do they focus on generating support for a future referendum? Or do they splinter off and create their own party — a real, powerful separatist party?" Bratt said. ($1 = 1.4137 Canadian dollars)

item.title: Nasdaq climbs over 1% as AI-linked stocks recover ahead of key earnings
item.description: The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite led Wall Street's gains on Monday as investors returned to AI-related stocks following last week's bruising selloff, while declining oil prices lent additional support ahead of key corporate earnings reports.
item.dc:creator: Tharuniyaa Lakshmi, Ragini Mathur
item.content:encoded: The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite led Wall Street's gains on Monday as investors returned to AI-related stocks following last week's bruising selloff, while declining oil prices lent additional support ahead of key corporate earnings reports. The benchmark S&P 500 and Nasdaq had posted their biggest weekly drop since late June on Friday, as concerns that higher interest rates could curb investments in AI infrastructure weighed on technology stocks, particularly data center operators. The selloff reflected mounting investor unease over how the costly AI build-out will be financed, a question that has increasingly pressured companies underpinning the US bull market, which [USN:L6N45R12W TEXT:"recently marked its fourth anniversary"]. CoreWeave (CRWV.O) , which was at the center of last week's selloff after its shares [USN:L4N4620ZT TEXT:"plunged more than 25%"] on worries over a $50 billion debt load, climbed 3.1% on Monday. Goldman Sachs upgraded the neocloud firm to "buy" from "neutral", saying the recent selloff offers a buying opportunity. Peers Nebius (NBIS.O) and Iren (IREN.O) gained 4.7% and 6.5%, respectively. Chipmakers Broadcom (AVGO.O) climbed 3.2% and Micron (MU.O) jumped 5.3%. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (.SOX) rose 3.7%, putting it on course to end an eight-day losing streak, its longest run of declines since October 2008. Amazon.com (AMZN.O) was up 5.2% after Morgan Stanley named the e-commerce and cloud computing firm as its "top pick". "The main concern was CoreWeave and the potential for the yields on their bonds going up and the liquidity issues there. That certainly scared people," said Joe Saluzzi, co-head of equity trading at Themis Trading. "Looks like this morning they've settled down, and I think the trade still seems to have legs." Focus is now shifting to a busy week of corporate earnings, with Meta (META.O) expected to beat Wall Street expectations on Wednesday. Elon Musk-led Tesla's (TSLA.O) results are also due that day, while SpaceX (SPCX.O) is scheduled to report on Tuesday. At 11:42 a.m. ET, the Dow Jones Industrial Average (.DJI) rose 91.03 points, or 0.18%, to 52,093.44. The S&P 500 (.SPX) gained 68.47 points, or 0.89%, to 7,727.91, while the Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) advanced 463.92 points, or 1.78%, to 26,603.96. The session coincides with the 39th anniversary of Black Monday, the 1987 crash that marked the biggest one-day decline in the history of Dow Jones Industrial Average. Of the 11 S&P 500 constituents, five posted losses. However, consumer discretionary (.SPLRCT) and technology group (.SPLRCT) led the gains, up 2.8% and 2.2%, respectively. Brent futures were last down 1.7% at around $108 a barrel, following US President Donald Trump's decision to [USN:L6N464042 TEXT:"waive some sanctions"] on Russia. Intel (INTC.O) shares rose 5.8% after [USN:L6N4650J6 TEXT:"J.P.Morgan upgraded"] the stock to "neutral" from "underweight." Cleveland-Cliffs (CLF.N) surged 15.6% after the steelmaker surpassed analysts' estimate for third-quarter profit. Declining issues outnumbered advancers by 1.11-to-1 ratio on the NYSE, while advancing issues outnumbered decliners by 1.28-to-1 ratio on the Nasdaq. The S&P 500 posted 10 new 52-week highs and two new lows, and the Nasdaq Composite recorded 20 new highs and 242 new lows.

item.title: Uber wins bid to throw out UK mass lawsuit by black cab drivers
item.description: Uber won its bid on Monday to throw out two linked lawsuits seeking around £340 million ($453 million) brought by thousands of London black cab drivers and two former private hire companies.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Uber (UBER.N) won its bid on Monday to throw out two linked lawsuits seeking around £340 million ($453 million) brought by thousands of London black cab drivers and two former private hire companies. The ride-hailing app was sued in 2024 over allegations about how it obtained a private hire vehicle operating licence in the British capital, with the claimants alleging Uber gave "misleading and inaccurate information" to Transport for London. The lawsuits at London's High Court sought damages of nearly £200 million for around 13,000 black cab drivers, while a claimant suing on behalf of two now-defunct companies, Kabbie and Iride, was seeking around £140 million. Uber denied the allegations and also argued the lawsuits were filed after the six-year limitation period for bringing such a claim, meaning they should be thrown out. Judge Simon Birt said in a written ruling that the claimants could have discovered the alleged deception before 2018, six years before the lawsuits were filed, and dismissed the claims on the limitation grounds without considering the merits. "We are pleased that the court has dismissed all of these claims entirely at the earliest opportunity and the ruling today has put these legacy matters firmly in the past," an Uber spokesperson said. The lawsuits focused on the information Uber provided to Transport for London when it first became licenced as a private hire operator in 2012. The company has since taken much of the business of traditional black cab drivers. "We are obviously very disappointed and are considering all options available to the claimant cab drivers with the legal team," said a spokesperson for RGL Management, which managed the lawsuits on behalf of the claimants. Monday's ruling comes ahead of an even larger case involving Uber in London, with the company fighting the British tax authority in a more than [USN:L8N42K0FO TEXT:"£1 billion tax dispute"]. (This story has been corrected to remove the reference to 'next week,' in the third bullet point and in paragraph 9.)

item.title: European shares slip as France unrest dents sentiment
item.description: French equities suffered their worst day in nearly two weeks on Monday, weighing on European shares after rioting erupted in cities across the country over the weekend.
item.dc:creator: Avinash P, Niket Nishant
item.content:encoded: French equities suffered their worst day in nearly two weeks on Monday, weighing on European shares after [USN:L1N46401W TEXT:"rioting erupted"] in cities across the country over the weekend. France's blue-chip CAC 40 index (.FCHI) fell 1.1%, while the pan-European STOXX 600 index (.STOXX) slipped 0.9% to 639.1 points. Triggered by rising prices and worsening public services, the protests have soured investor sentiment towards a country already grappling with weak growth and rising debt. The turmoil in the euro zone's second-largest economy, which adds to political uncertainty ahead of the presidential election in 2027, has also been partly responsible for keeping the STOXX 600 index stuck within a narrow range over the past month. "There is clearly political risk and that is going to mean you get near-term volatility," said Kiran Ganesh, a multi-asset strategist at UBS Global Wealth Management. French lenders BNP Paribas (BNPP.PA) , Societe Generale (SOGN.PA) and Credit Agricole (CAGR.PA) fell between 2.5% and 3.4%. Retailer Carrefour (CARR.PA) declined 2.2% and shopping mall operator Unibail-Rodamco-Westfield (URW.PA) dropped 2%. SPAIN'S POLITICAL RISKS SPARK CAUTION Political uncertainty also came to the fore in Spain, where the equities benchmark (.IBEX) fell 1.5%. A snap election scheduled for next month has left investors wary. Spain's hard-left parties on Saturday [USN:L8N46305T TEXT:"presented"] separate candidate lists for the election, reducing Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez's chances of staying in power at the head of a leftist coalition. "Spain faces its own political constraints around budgets and fiscal reforms, although stronger economic growth provides some protection," said Daniela Hathorn, senior market analyst at Capital.com. Cyclical sectors led declines across Europe, with banks (.SX7E) the biggest laggards following a 2.2% decline. Defence stocks (.SXPARO) also came under pressure, falling 1.5%. The technology index (.SX8P) was the only major index in positive territory, rising 0.7%. Last week, European shares held up better than US peers during a selloff in AI-linked stocks over concerns about rising debt to fund infrastructure spending. Investors were also awaiting earnings from European and US blue-chip companies. Software maker SAP (SAPG.DE) , British lender Barclays (BARC.L) and telecom equipment maker Nokia (NOKIA.HE) are scheduled to report later this week. In the US, results from Meta Platforms (META.O) and chip firms could provide fresh direction for equity markets. Among individual movers, Barclays (BARC.L) dropped 3.5% to hit its lowest since mid June. The Bank of England is examining whether Barclays traders [USN:L6N4650GN TEXT:"misrepresented illiquid private credit loans"] to understate their risk after an insider at the British bank raised concerns, the Financial Times reported, citing people familiar with the matter. Norway's Mowi (MOWI.OL) gained 3.5% after the salmon producer's third-quarter harvest volumes hit an all-time high.

item.title: Spain's rush to clear Ceuta migrant backlog raises rights concerns
item.description: When heavily pregnant Fatna and her disabled son arrived in Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta during a chaotic mass border crossing on July 30, she hoped to be high on authorities' list for help.
item.dc:creator: Corina Pons, Victoria Waldersee
item.content:encoded: When heavily pregnant Fatna and her disabled son arrived in Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta during a [USN:L8N44F14U TEXT:"chaotic mass border crossing"] on July 30, she hoped to be high on authorities' list for help. Nearly three months later, with her newborn baby girl suffering from kidney problems, Fatna, 21, and her family urgently need to reach mainland Spain for specialist hospital treatment. However, travelling while her asylum claim is under review requires a permit that Spain's socialist government – ordinarily a staunch advocate of immigration – has been reluctant to grant to any of the thousands of migrants remaining in Ceuta. Some are still scattered on the streets or hiding in the rolling hills of the tiny 20-sq-km port city on Morocco's northeast border. Unaccompanied minors evicted over the weekend from an industrial estate near the border with Morocco were documented in local media sleeping on the pavement in front of the police headquarters, waiting to be registered. Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez's government is under pressure from the EU and an increasingly frustrated populace to sort out the crisis and faces [USN:L8N45R05N TEXT:"a snap election"] on November 29. It [USN:L8N45L09S TEXT:"is working on shortcuts"] for asylum applications with the intention of sending most people home, mainly to Morocco, on the basis of being economic migrants not real asylum-seekers. That, NGOs fear, risks violating migrants' rights. More than 20 interviews by Reuters with migrants, lawyers, NGOs, and security forces revealed that many of those who remain have clear grounds for asylum or humanitarian protection: from unaccompanied minors to LGBT Moroccans fearing imprisonment if deported and families like Fatna's classified as vulnerable under EU law. Last week, eight charities including Oxfam and Amnesty International filed a complaint with Spain's ombudsman seen by Reuters alleging "grave rights violations" in the tiny Ceuta enclave. They included the forced return of migrants from conflict-hit countries and denial of interpreters and legal assistance. Spokespeople for Spain's central government, interior ministry, territorial policy ministry and migration ministry did not respond to Reuters requests for comment on the mistreatment accusations. Sanchez, one of Europe's few remaining left-leaning leaders, said last week that Spain was managing the flood of cases "responsibly, with a sense of solidarity and respecting migrants' human rights". "There are people who will truly be in enormous danger if they are returned to Morocco," said Wendell Soares, coordinator of the Catholic migrant reception centre San Antonio which has taken in Fatna's family and dozens more vulnerable people, far beyond its usual capacity of seven. "When the word 'immigrant' is used, it creates a collective image, as if they were all the same. Every person has their own story." DEPORTED WITHOUT EXPLANATION Spanish right-wing and far-right parties were already angry with Sanchez's government for [USN:L8N42N0Y2 TEXT:"providing legal status"] to nearly 1 million irregular migrants earlier this year. They have cast July's crossing as a deliberate invasion by Morocco – an accusation Morocco denies – and demanded that all migrants be returned . But despite plans for a [USN:S8N4150LX TEXT:"new EU-wide procedure"] enabling accelerated deportations in future emergency scenarios, current rules require that migrants be assessed case-by-case. While most are from Morocco, the government estimated in August that more than 1,000 of the migrants remaining were from sub-Saharan countries whose nationals are granted asylum in over 90% of cases in Spain, according to government statistics. The EU's [USN:L8N42J0LA TEXT:"new pact"] requires that cases be processed in border zones to permit faster deportations. But it does not require applicants to stay where they arrived, allowing for transfers to other border zones in Spain that would alleviate pressure on the 84,000-person enclave of Ceuta, Europe's only land border with Africa. If vulnerable migrants' cases are to be properly assessed, such transfers are the "only option", said Juan Miguel Morales, director-general of NGO Sur Acoge. While 262 minors have been transferred to the Spanish mainland since the July crossing, the government's strategy for the remaining adults has been to convince as many as possible to return of their own volition. The government said this week that 12,000 had chosen to cross back since mid-August. "There are no covert deportations under any circumstances," Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said, describing the returns as voluntary and adding that up to 1,200 asylum applications had been received and 700 of them resolved. However, at least nine NGOs have in public communication or interviews with Reuters claimed that migrants they support were coerced to return. Asociación Elin said migrants from Sudan and Chad were summoned by police on September 24 and 25 and deported without warning, according to the complaint to the ombudsman. In text messages reviewed by Reuters, Moroccan migrant Azhaar Chaouni told volunteers at German NGO Mission Lifeline that he and other migrants faced the same fate, after being picked up in buses by police from their makeshift camps on the beach and told they were being taken to reception centres. "They deported us without explanation," Chaouni wrote, saying he was in Morocco. Morocco's designation as a "safe country of origin" under EU rules does not strip its citizens of the right to apply for asylum, said Andrea de Petris, immigration expert at the think tank CEP, based in Freiburg, Germany. "Each individual must be guaranteed a specific assessment of their personal circumstances," added De Petris who estimates the procedure would inevitably be "lengthy and costly". Stories of others disappearing have instilled fear in Rayane, a 19-year-old gay Moroccan awaiting news on his asylum application in the San Antonio reception centre. Rejected by his family and unable to live openly in Morocco where same-sex sexual acts are prosecuted, he is desperate to get to mainland Europe. "I can’t even imagine myself going back to Morocco. I’d kill myself before even crossing the border," he said. PACT EXPOSED Frontline workers and NGOs on the ground say the situation in Ceuta has proven that the 12-week limit set in the EU’s migrant pact for processing asylum applications is unrealistic, with seven stating they expect the process to drag on for months. A lack of resources from staff to functioning computers meant that only around 100 migrants' cases were being registered daily by October 14, according to police union representative Raul Piera. The union estimates roughly 7,000-8,000 more migrants are still scattered across the city, sleeping rough or squeezed into facilities provided by charities and civil society groups filling the gap left by Ceuta's overwhelmed social services. "Looking at the remaining workload, this will last well into next summer," said Piera. Spain's government has declined to comment on estimates of unregistered migrants, with Territorial Policy Minister Angel Victor Torres telling reporters on October 14 that it was impossible to know how many were hiding. Doctors in Ceuta's only hospital are treating migrants for scabies, tuberculosis and gastrointestinal infections caused by long periods outdoors, said Enrique Robiralta, head of the doctors' union. At least seven women have given birth. Fatna and her husband Mohamed are desperate to stay in Spain, fearing for the new baby and convinced their 3-year-old disabled son will die in Morocco. "We are doing everything for our son," said Mohamed.

item.title: France urges curfews in some areas after weekend of riots
item.description: France's central government asked some local authorities to impose curfews as it faced pressure over security failings on Monday after a weekend of riots and looting stemming from nationwide anti-government protests.
item.dc:creator: Sudip Kar-Gupta, Elizabeth Pineau
item.content:encoded: France's central government asked some local authorities to impose curfews as it faced pressure over security failings on Monday after a [USN:L1N46401W TEXT:"weekend of riots and looting"] stemming from nationwide anti-government protests. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu ruled out a blanket curfew in Paris but not a state of emergency. But he said it was more appropriate for now to apply partial and localised curfews, without providing details. "My determination to restore order is absolute," he told reporters. Ariel Weil, the Socialist mayor of central Paris, said on BFM TV he favoured a curfew. Marseille banned gatherings and demonstrations. French unions meanwhile called for a new round of strikes and rallies on November 5. The [USN:L1N4650EF TEXT:"weekend of looting"] and violence between some protesters and police followed weeks of student demonstrations, rocking France six months ahead of its [USN:L6N4650JF TEXT:"next presidential election"] and highlighting pressures from a weak economy and surging debt. MINISTER BLAMES FAR LEFT Lecornu blamed far-left groups for some of France's worst unrest in years. "There is, after all, a far-left movement that wants to cause — we can’t put it any more strongly — profound unrest in the country in the run-up to the presidential election," he said. Hard-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon urged him to provide evidence. "Otherwise, he should apologise, keep quiet and stop fanning the flames of unrest," he said on X. The Federation of Trade and Retail said almost 3,000 shops had been affected over the weekend. "Once again, the retail sector finds itself on the front line, at a time when it is already weakened by a succession of crises," it said. "Behind every ransacked shop are business owners, employees and families who have seen years of work and effort wiped out in a matter of hours," it added, calling for social security and tax relief for affected businesses. Lecornu said the government would provide furlough measures from Tuesday. Standing before a boarded-up shopfront, Gerard Nouchi, manager of two clothing stores in Marseille, said there weren't enough police to stop the looters. "They trashed everything, broke things, insulted us,” Nouchi said. "It was like a real tornado." The government ordered platforms selling looted goods to take down announcements and collaborate to prosecute resellers, Junior Digital Minister Anne Le Hénanff wrote on X. Some 2,400 people were arrested and one protester died from a cardiac arrest on Saturday while nearly 1,000 officers were injured, according to the Interior Ministry. 'LEFT WITHOUT PROTECTION' French assets [USN:L1N46507D TEXT:"were underperforming"] broader European markets on Monday, though moves were more contained than at some other moments of recent political friction. Tensions in President Emmanuel Macron's fragile government over apparent security shortcomings — coming as the government needs to pass a budget bill to rein in its finances — could further [USN:L8N46508Y TEXT:"unsettle investors"]. Macron's office said on Monday he had turned down his Interior Minister Laurent Nunez's offer to resign, telling him instead to put an end to barricades and looting and be transparent over what Macron called "intelligence and foresight failings". Nunez told reporters that Tuesday evening's Champions League soccer match between Paris Saint-Germain and Barcelona would go ahead as planned. The mayors of Paris, Marseille and Lyon said in a joint op-ed in the newspaper Liberation that they were used to demonstrations and protests. "But on Saturday ... for the first time, we had the feeling that whole sections of our cities had been left without protection," said the mayors, all from the centre-left. The start of school holidays on Monday may provide relief, but students were staging more gatherings and blockades in some places, including the Louvre gallery and Sciences Po university in central Paris. LUXURY BOUTIQUES DAMAGED At the weekend, hundreds of thousands took to the streets to protest over what many say are declining and dysfunctional public services. At the Place Vendome in Paris, home to luxury hotels and boutiques, most shops were shuttered and surrounded by security guards on Monday. The front door of a Dior boutique was smashed, while windows belonging to other luxury brand stores in central Paris, including Rolex, Louis Vuitton, Ralph Lauren and Gucci, were damaged. In Marseille, Ligue 1 club [USN:L4N4650P2 TEXT:"Olympique de Marseille"] said its official store on the city's historic main avenue had been looted, while a town hall in central France [USN:L1N46402C TEXT:"was torched"]. France deployed 60,000 police and other security forces on Saturday, Nunez told France Inter radio, but he acknowledged that was not enough to control violent crowds. Cost-of-living issues also drove weekend protests in other European countries including [USN:L8N463090 TEXT:"Italy"], [USN:L6N46303L TEXT:"Belgium"] and [USN:L6N4620YF TEXT:"Albania"]. European governments [USN:L8N4650JR TEXT:"have advised"] citizens travelling to France to avoid large crowds and exercise caution. As France was busy cleaning up its streets, Macron arrived in Kuwait for a Gulf trip aimed at securing additional petrol and diesel supplies to bring down pump prices.

item.title: UBS capital rules have Swiss stuck between a rock and a hard place
item.description: Swiss lawmakers face a quandary as they craft new capital rules for UBS following the 2023 collapse of Credit Suisse: too strict and Switzerland's biggest bank might move abroad, too lax and a potential referendum could prolong the uncertainty.
item.dc:creator: Dave Graham, Ariane Luthi
item.content:encoded: Swiss lawmakers face a quandary as they craft new capital rules for UBS (UBSG.S) following the 2023 collapse of Credit Suisse: too strict and Switzerland's biggest bank might move abroad, too lax and a potential referendum could prolong the uncertainty. A lower house committee will on October 26 begin debating banking rules [USN:L8N45F0DE TEXT:"passed"] last month by the Swiss upper house of parliament that management at UBS [USN:L1N45C05I TEXT:"suggested"] were intolerable. Prospects for lighter touch rules emerging appear slim. Major investors have [USN:L2N3VH0C3 TEXT:"urged"] UBS to leave Switzerland in search of friendlier regulation, and the bank is drafting potential contingency plans including shifting its headquarters or merging with another lender, [USN:L8N46120Y TEXT:"sources"] told Reuters. Yet the cost of leaving or loss of its Swiss identity [USN:L1N45I046 TEXT:"might"] be a price the Zurich-based wealth manager is unwilling to pay. Leo Mueller, a Centre Party lawmaker on the committee, said parliament was in a tricky situation. "If we water it down too much, there'll be a referendum. Then there's a risk people say 'it's not enough', it gets rejected and we end up with nothing at all," he said. "If we're too strict, the bank could say, 'Well, Switzerland is now a tough place to do business, we'll look elsewhere.'" Compromises are circulating, with some lawmakers working to temper the proposals, but the view across the political spectrum is that any softening will be challenging. REFERENDUM THREAT The upper house decided UBS should back its foreign units with 90% Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital, up from a current 60% buffer that can be partly met with cheaper capital. The government proposed a 100% CET1 requirement. UBS has repeatedly said it wants to remain in Switzerland and that its presence there is beneficial to both the bank and the country. However, it argues the 90% CET1 proposal is excessive and would damage its competitiveness. Finance Minister Karin Keller-Sutter, who has [USN:L6N44T0K0 TEXT:"hinted"] at the possibility of a public referendum, in which a law can be challenged with enough support, wants parliament to sign off on the 90% CET1 target, a person familiar with the matter said. Her ministry declined to comment. The Social Democrats, who favour 100% CET1 capital, say they will decide whether to seek a referendum once parliament has made its choice, which is not expected before December at the earliest. Some shareholders say the proposed rules could suffocate UBS. [USN:L1N45N061 TEXT:"Artisan Partners"] has publicly urged it to quit Switzerland over the regulations. Hans-Peter Portmann of the centre-right Liberal Party, or FDP, has floated a 75% CET1 capital requirement for UBS' foreign units, combined with a mechanism to bolster its loss-absorbing capacity if capital ratios go below a certain level. "A solution will be found that enables UBS to keep compensating shareholders for risk appropriately and to set aside investment capital for the future, while minimizing the default risk for the Swiss public as far as possible," he said. Other proposals are likely to surface ahead of the full lower house debate expected in December. TOUGHER LINE Upper house support for the 90% CET1 proposal was stronger than [USN:L8N45G13W TEXT:"expected"]. In the lower house, left-of-centre parties are better represented and those on the centre and centre-right are either split or leaning towards a firmer line, people within parliament told Reuters. "My personal view is the lower house could settle on 90%," said FDP lawmaker Olivier Feller, who supports 100% CET1 backing of UBS' foreign units but said his party's stance was still under discussion. "We're a small country with a large bank." Urs Saxer, a University of Zurich law professor, said any compromise would likely end up close to the 90% CET1 proposal. "UBS will not act irrationally," he said. "One would need a very good reason to leave, and the stability and legal certainty Switzerland offer are not easy to find nowadays."

item.title: L'Ukraine pas avertie de nouvelles frappes russes, qui ont fait quatre morts - Zelensky
item.description: La Russie a de nouveau frappé Kyiv et ses environs sans que l'Ukraine n'ait été avertie au préalable, a déclaré le président du pays Volodimir Zelensky, qui a également fait état d'un retard de livraisons d'équipements essentiels en provenance des Etats-Unis.
item.dc:creator: Olena Harmash
item.content:encoded: La Russie a de nouveau frappé Kyiv et ses environs sans que l'Ukraine n'ait été avertie au préalable, a déclaré le président du pays Volodimir Zelensky, qui a également fait état d'un retard de livraisons d'équipements essentiels en provenance des Etats-Unis. Il a ajouté que cette nouvelle attaque lancée par Moscou, l'une des plus importantes de ces derniers mois, avait visé des infrastructures énergétiques, privant plus de 550.000 foyers d'électricité. La Russie a lancé 16 missiles balistiques sur la capitale ukrainienne, ainsi que plus de 200 drones, l'attaque s'étendant de Kharkiv et Dnipro, dans l'est du pays, jusqu'à Odessa au sud et dans les régions de Volhynie et de Rivne à l'ouest. Plus de 10 infrastructures énergétiques ont été endommagées, a poursuivi Volodimir Zelensky. Quatre personnes ont été tuées : deux et à Kyiv et dans sa région et deux à Kryvyï Rih, ont dit de leur côté les autorités régionales. "Une nouvelle attaque russe avec des missiles balistiques s'est déroulée en plusieurs vagues cette nuit et, une fois de plus, nos partenaires ne nous ont pas donné d'alerte précoce", a dit le président ukrainien sur la messagerie Telegram. "Lorsque les livraisons de missiles destinés à la défense aérienne de l'Ukraine sont bloquées et que de son côté la Russie bénéficie d'allègements ou de reports de sanctions, cela revient malheureusement à un déni de réalité de la part de nos partenaires", a poursuivi Volodimir Zelensky. Dimanche, il avait pourtant déclaré que les Etats-Unis, après une brève pause, avaient repris le [USN:L6N46403X TEXT:"partage"] de renseignements avec l'Ukraine pour l'aider à se défendre contre les attaques de missiles russes. L'Ukraine s'appuie sur les renseignements satellitaires américains pour repérer les missiles tirés quotidiennement par la Russie contre ses villes. Le président ukrainien a également dit que les États-Unis avaient ralenti la livraison de certains équipements essentiels destinés à l'Ukraine, ajoutant que ces retards étaient le fait du ministère américain de la Défense sans fournir aucun autre détail. Cela fait des mois que l'Ukraine souffre d'une pénurie missiles d'interception Patriot, de fabrication américaine, équipement indispensable pour contrer des missiles balistiques. Le ministère de la Défense russe a déclaré de son côté que ses forces avaient mené une "frappe massive" sur Kyiv et sa région, précisant que cette attaque a visé des sites militaro-industriels, des centres de données ainsi que des entrepôts de missiles de croisière et de drones. Le président américain Donald Trump a annoncé vendredi la levée de plusieurs sanctions, restrictions et droits de douane visant la Russie. Et, il y a une semaine, il annoncé un [USN:L8N45V1O6 TEXT:"accord"], conclu entre Washington et Moscou, concernant l'approvisionnement en diesel. Le maire de Kyiv Vitali Klitschko a précisé que les frappes russes avaient touché une station de métro de la capitale, un immeuble résidentiel de 25 étages, des bâtiments non résidentiels et un établissement médical.

item.title: World faces nature reality check at UN biodiversity conference
item.description: World leaders, diplomats and nature experts gather in Armenia this week to assess lagging efforts to halt biodiversity loss, with countries off track on most global targets and divisions over funding still unresolved.
item.dc:creator: Virginia Furness
item.content:encoded: World leaders, diplomats and nature experts gather in Armenia this week to assess lagging efforts to halt biodiversity loss, with countries off track on most global targets and divisions over funding still unresolved. The 17th UN "Conference of the Parties", dubbed COP17, is the first major review of progress under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, the landmark 2022 agreement that aims to protect 30% of land and sea by 2030. The climate-focused COP31 begins on November 9 in Antalya, Turkey. While the world is likely to reach an estimated 27.5% of land protection by 2030, scientists say many of the broader goals needed to halt biodiversity loss remain well off track. From pesticide use to unsustainable fishing and subsidies for a host of damaging activities, the deterioration of ecosystems threatens food production, water security and economic stability across the planet. Countries are currently not on track to meet 22 of the 23 goals set out in the Kunming-Montreal framework, a draft UN report showed. While the UN says 144 countries including Brazil and China have so far created action plans, who pays and how much towards a $30 billion public finance goal is less clear and will be central to two weeks of talks in Armenia's capital Yerevan. The broader goal is to mobilise at least $200 billion per year by 2030. SUBSIDY REFORM Another major focus is reforming $500 billion a year of subsidies for activities that damage nature, with governments urged to set a two-year timeline to identify and redirect the most damaging ones. That could, for example, include those that encourage farmers to cut down rainforest or the offer of state discounts on synthetic fertilisers and chemical pesticides which damage soil and water. Doing so would help governments address nature loss and related issues like food and energy security without committing more public money at a time of war, energy crises and other inflationary pressures. "This isn't primarily a story about conservation," said Eva Zabey, CEO of the non-profit Business for Nature at a media briefing. "It's an economic, fiscal, political and competitiveness story, which is grounded in resilience and resource security." More than 130 businesses including retailer H&M (HMb.ST) and consumer goods company Nestle (NESN.S) issued an open letter ahead of the talks urging governments to set clearer policies and a plan to reform incentives over the next 12 months, arguing that it would help make it more attractive to invest. Subsidies ultimately cost governments between $11 trillion and $24.7 trillion a year, non-profit Conservation International estimates, as they often pay twice - once for the subsidies and again to patch up the damage that follows including cleaning up pollution, treating illness and repairing infrastructure. BIGGER ROLE FOR PRIVATE SECTOR With public money tight, many are looking to the private sector to play a bigger role, including through the Cali Fund. That fund was set up in 2025 to get companies which rely on digital databases of biological samples for their products, such as in the pharmaceutical, cosmetic and commercial agriculture industries, to help pay to preserve nature. Details still to be ironed out include how funds should be shared between countries and Indigenous communities, and whether companies should contribute based on total revenue when only part of their business relies on these genetic resources. For Cristián Samper, managing director and leader of Nature Solutions at the Bezos Earth Fund, the talks are also an opportunity for governments to do more to halt the extinction of species. "We know recovery is possible. The decisions we make in Armenia should give more conservation teams the backing to make it happen," he said.

item.title: Gold edges lower as firm dollar, elevated yields weigh
item.description: Gold prices edged lower on Monday, pressured by a firm dollar and elevated US Treasury yields, while investors awaited the Federal Reserve's policy decision next week, when officials are expected to leave interest rates unchanged.
item.dc:creator: Anushree Mukherjee, Vishak Mathew
item.content:encoded: Gold prices edged lower on Monday, pressured by a firm dollar and elevated US Treasury yields, while investors awaited the Federal Reserve's policy decision next week, when officials are expected to leave interest rates unchanged. Spot gold fell 0.5% to $4,143.91 per ounce by 11:34 a.m. EDT (1534 GMT). US gold futures for December delivery were down 0.4% at $4,163.30 per ounce. The US dollar edged up, making greenback-denominated gold more expensive for holders of other currencies, and 10-year US Treasury yields rose 0.6%. "There are concerns that central banks will have to tighten their policies further to control inflation, which is providing yields another boost. And with yields remaining elevated, gold investors are wondering whether it makes more sense to be in the bond market right now" said Fawad Razaqzada, market analyst at Forex.com. The Fed raised interest rates by a quarter point in September, its first hike this year. "It is not just about whether the Fed hikes next week or waits until December; the tone of its guidance will matter. A hawkish message could bring further short-term weakness for gold," Razaqzada added. According to the CME's FedWatch Tool , traders see an 82.8% chance that the Fed will leave rates unchanged this month, while expectations for a hike in December remain at 90%. FEDWATCH While gold is typically considered a hedge against inflation, higher interest rates reduce the appeal of the non-yielding asset. Investors are also awaiting US Personal Consumption Expenditures data next week, the central bank's preferred gauge of inflation. Meanwhile, oil prices slipped from a five-month high after US President Donald Trump waived sanctions and tariffs on Russia that may lead to more Russian fuel exports. The drop in oil prices eased some inflation concerns after strong US [USN:L1N45Z121 TEXT:"CPI"] and [USN:L1N4610KT TEXT:"PPI"] readings last week. "In our view, key resistance remains at $4,235, while support continues to emerge below $4,100," said Ole Hansen, head of commodity strategy at Saxo Bank. Among other metals, spot silver gained 0.4% to $57.24 per ounce, platinum rose 1% to $1,646 per ounce and palladium climbed 0.8% to $1,121.14 per ounce.

item.title: Zelenskiy says Ukraine got no warning as Russian missiles rain in
item.description: Ukraine received no advance warning from its partners of a Russian ballistic missile strike overnight, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Monday, adding that some vital deliveries from the United States were being delayed.
item.dc:creator: Olena Harmash
item.content:encoded: Ukraine received no advance warning from its partners of a Russian ballistic missile strike overnight, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Monday, adding that some vital deliveries from the United States were being delayed. Moscow launched one of its broadest air assaults in months overnight, cutting power to more than half a million households and damaging energy infrastructure across Ukraine. Russia fired 16 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and the surrounding region and more than 200 drones in attacks stretching from Kharkiv and Dnipro in the east to Odesa in the south and Volyn and Rivne in the west. The strikes killed two people in Kyiv and the nearby region and two more people in the industrial city of Kryvyi Rih, officials said. Tensions are running high between Zelenskiy and President Donald Trump's administration over US support for Ukraine and Washington's approach to Russia. "Another Russian ballistic missile attack came in several waves overnight, and once again, there was no early warning from our partners," Zelenskiy said on the Telegram app. "When deliveries of missiles for Ukraine's air defence are blocked while Russia is granted relief or delays in sanctions, this is, unfortunately, a denial of reality on the part of our partners." Zelenskiy said that the United States had slowed some vital supplies for Ukraine, adding that the delays were at the US Defense Department level. He provided no other details. Kyiv has previously said it has struggled to get interceptors critical to repelling Russian missile attacks. For several months, Ukraine has suffered from critical shortages of US-made Patriot missiles. Zelenskiy said that some political agreements on air defence were not implemented at a working level. Throughout the nearly five-year war, Ukraine has relied on US intelligence to detect Russian ballistic missile launches and provide early warning of incoming strikes. Yurii Ihnat, a spokesman for the Ukrainian air force, said Kyiv received no warning ahead of the first ballistic missile strike overnight but did receive information ahead of a second attack. "For some reason, no information was received the first time, a matter our experts are investigating together with our partners, as this is not the first time such a situation has occurred," Ihnat told Ukrainian television. Secretary of State Marco Rubio [USN:L1N465065 TEXT:"denied"] that the United States had paused some intelligence sharing with Ukraine. ROLLING BLACKOUTS Ukrainian air defences downed 247 targets - four cruise missiles and 243 drones, the air force said. Russia's Defence Ministry said its forces carried out a "massive strike" using precision weapons and attack drones against Ukrainian defence industry facilities, drone and cruise missile storage sites, and a data centre. Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said the energy sector was the main target of the attacks, with damage reported across the country. Ukraine's energy ministry said rolling blackouts were introduced for households and businesses as crews worked to restore supplies. Koretskyi said Russia has hit Ukrainian energy infrastructure more than 2,000 times since mid-July, intensifying its attacks from previous years of the war. Railway and metro stations, pharmaceutical warehouses, commercial properties and residential buildings were also damaged, Koretskyi said. Ukrainian businesses have already lost $7.7 billion due to wartime damage so far this year, he said. "The aim is obvious — to wear people down," Koretskyi said.

item.title: US stocks rebound with AI earnings test ahead; French markets tumble
item.description: The Nasdaq was up more than 1% in early trading on Monday as tech shares rebounded ahead of a big week for AI-related earnings, while French markets and the euro fell as unrest in France added to concerns about the country's fiscal outlook.
item.dc:creator: Caroline Valetkevitch, Danilo Masoni
item.content:encoded: The Nasdaq was up more than 1% in early trading on Monday as tech shares rebounded ahead of a big week for AI-related earnings, while [USN:L6N4650X5 TEXT:"French markets"] and the euro fell as unrest in France added to concerns about the country's fiscal outlook. French bonds, Paris-listed stocks and the euro also fell as the widespread protests across France underscored the difficulties the government faces in reducing its large deficit. Wall Street stocks recovered some ground after a bruising week, with an index of semiconductors (.SOX) up 3.6%. On Friday, the index sank in its eighth straight day of declines, its longest losing streak since 2008. With results due from Meta (META.O) on Wednesday, and results from Tesla (TSLA.O) and chipmakers Lam Research (LRCX.O) and Texas Instruments (TXN.O) also due this week, investors will be watching for signs that massive AI spending ultimately pays off. "Investors are buying the correction dip that we had," said Peter Cardillo, chief market economist at Spartan Capital Securities in New York. "The market is now going to go through a very critical test over the next two weeks. We have some big name earnings coming out," he said. "In terms of technology, the test of whether or not the spending on AI... will be met with satisfaction is going to be critical." The Dow Jones Industrial Average (.DJI) rose 45.31 points, or 0.08%, to 52,045.44, the S&P 500 (.SPX) rose 56.93 points, or 0.74%, to 7,716.13 and the Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) rose 398.49 points, or 1.52%, to 26,538.53. MSCI's gauge of stocks across the globe (.MIWD00000PUS) rose 2.85 points, or 0.25%, to 1,131.95. Meta is one of five AI hyperscalers expected to increase combined capital expenditure to about $1.2 trillion next year, according to Goldman Sachs. Results from SpaceX (SPCX.O) are also due on Tuesday. Overall, US earnings are still expected to rise about 30%, largely driven by the technology sector. A recent bond selloff also unsettled technology stocks and intensified scrutiny of the AI sector's massive funding needs. [USN:L6N4650Z6 TEXT:"US Treasury yields"] edged higher on Monday, with the benchmark 10-year Treasury yield coming off its biggest weekly drop in seven months, as concerns about the impact of higher interest rates on AI stocks eased. Recent comments from Federal Reserve officials, including Chairman Kevin Warsh, suggest policymakers are in no rush to hike rates again. On Friday, Warsh expressed optimism about US economic strength but gave no indication of whether or when more hikes will be needed. In Europe, the pan-European STOXX 600 (.STOXX) index fell 1.04%, while France's blue-chip CAC 40 index (.FCHI) was down 1.4%. France's 10-year yield was up 13 basis points to 4.9% while the German 10-year yield, the benchmark for the euro zone, was also higher. [USN:L1N46401W TEXT:"Widespread weekend unrest"] in the euro zone's second-largest economy underscored the challenge facing the French government as it seeks to reduce its large budget deficit ahead of next year's presidential elections. EURO, OIL EASE The euro also fell against the dollar amid the turmoil in France. The euro was last down 0.22% at $1.1214. The dollar index , which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies including the yen and the euro, rose 0.14% to 101.94. The Australian dollar, meanwhile, was boosted after China's economic growth rebounded from three-year lows, expanding at a 4.5% annual pace in the third quarter. The Australian dollar strengthened 0.52% versus the greenback to $0.698. Oil prices eased as investors took profits after prices climbed to multi-month highs last week. Investors continued to keep a close eye on conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine. They assessed the impact of US waivers on some sanctions and tariffs affecting Russian exports. US crude fell 0.77% to $100.63 a barrel and Brent fell to $108.20 per barrel, down 1.49% on the day. Spot gold fell 0.51% to $4,143.79 an ounce.

item.title: Trump threatens California officials with imprisonment over stance on mail ballots
item.description: The Justice Dept. said election officials could be liable as abettors of a federal crime.
item.dc:creator: Jasper Ward
item.content:encoded: (This Oct 16 story has been repeated with no changes to the text.) The US Justice Department on Friday warned Los Angeles County and California election officials they could be liable as abettors of a federal crime if they count mail ballots returned by more than 20,000 people the Trump administration says are probably noncitizens. The warning to the Los Angeles County Assistant Counsel Peter Bollinger came less than three weeks before the November 3 midterm elections and days after the department gave California [USN:L6N460192 TEXT:"48 hours"] to review a list of alleged noncitizen voters or face legal action. On Thursday, the Justice Department [USN:L6N46117W TEXT:"sued California"] to block the state from counting the ballots. "Noncitizen voting in a federal election is a federal crime — and knowingly facilitating such conduct is equally unlawful," Trent McCotter, the acting US deputy attorney general, wrote in a letter released on Friday. McCotter called on the county and California's secretary of state to reconsider their refusal to take steps that the Trump administration argues are needed to deter voter fraud. US President Donald Trump shared the letter on Truth Social with the comment: "They will all go to jail for a long period of time!!!" California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder Dean Logan were copied on McCotter's letter. The county's counsel office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Weber's office referred Reuters to an earlier statement in which she said the Justice Department's attempts to "unlawfully gain access to states' protected voter data and purge voter rolls serve only to cause chaos and fuel public distrust in our elections." An earlier letter that McCotter sent on Tuesday to Weber and Logan said the Justice Department provided officials in Los Angeles County with a "password-protected thumb drive" with the names of people the federal government "believes are likely noncitizens" that were sent mail-in ballots from California. Los Angeles County Counsel Dawyn R. Harrison said on Thursday the county cannot comply with the Justice Department's requests because the Trump administration did not explain how the list was made. Friday's letter from McCotter said the Justice Department used "internal immigration records" and data matching. In July, Trump said his administration had uncovered [USN:L1N43I0TJ TEXT:"evidence"] of more than 275,000 non-citizens registered to vote, but it was not clear how many had actually voted. In some previous cases, systems intended to verify citizenship have mistakenly flagged some naturalized US citizens as noncitizens. Studies have found that noncitizens casting actual ballots is exceedingly uncommon. Since July, the Justice Department has [USN:L6N45F10R TEXT:"ramped up prosecutions"] of people accused of illegally voting while not holding US citizenship. The White House has also [USN:L6N45D0T4 TEXT:"pushed"] federal agencies to accelerate their review of at least 47 state voter rolls obtained by the Department of Homeland Security, according to an internal email seen by Reuters.

item.title: What does Alberta's referendum on separation from Canada mean?
item.description: Alberta is holding a nonbinding referendum on Monday to ask residents if they want to remain part of Canada, marking the first time the oil-rich province has ever put the question of separation to the public. Polls have consistently shown most Albertans — about 70% — want to stay in Canada, with roughly a quarter of residents supporting an independent Alberta.
item.dc:creator: Maria Cheng
item.content:encoded: Alberta is holding a nonbinding [USN:L6N41X1E1 TEXT:"referendum "]on Monday to ask residents if they want to remain part of Canada, marking the first time the oil-rich province has ever put the question of separation to the public. Polls have consistently shown most Albertans — about 70% — want to stay in Canada, with roughly a quarter of residents supporting an [USN:L6N42Y0YK TEXT:"independent Alberta."] WHAT WILL RESIDENTS BE ASKED? There are 10 questions, each with its own color-coded ballot. The last ballot voters see is question 10, on whether Alberta should remain a Canadian province or start the legal process required to hold a binding referendum on separation. A simple majority in favor of separation could trigger that process. There are [USN:L6N3ZF146 TEXT:"nine other nonbinding questions "]about immigration, access to provincial services — including education, social care and healthcare — and voter identification requirements. WHY IS ALBERTA HAVING THIS REFERENDUM? Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said in May it was “time to have a vote, understand the will of Albertans on this subject, and move on,” when she announced the government would add a question on separation. Smith’s decision followed months of campaigning by a small but vocal group of separatists, who argue Alberta’s energy wealth is subsidizing poorer parts of the country and that bureaucracy in Ottawa has stifled the province’s economy. Some members of the group had backed Smith's candidacy for premier. Smith says she voted for Alberta to remain in Canada during advance polling, according to a video she posted on social media on Wednesday. HAVE THERE BEEN PREVIOUS SEPARATIST REFERENDUMS IN CANADA? Yes, but not in Alberta. The majority French-speaking province of Quebec has had two referendums, in 1980 and 1995. Quebecers voted to remain in Canada both times, but by the slimmest of margins in 1995. The separatist Parti Quebecois won a provincial election [USN:L1N4590X4 TEXT:"earlier this month"] and has pledged to hold a third referendum, but only after US President Donald Trump has left office and if the party holds a majority. The PQ was elected with a minority government on October 5, meaning it will rely on smaller parties to pass legislation. Canada is a federation of 10 provinces and three territories. While Ottawa is responsible for matters of national interest, such as defense, trade and foreign policy, the provinces and territories hold significant power over medical care, education and land rights. WHEN WILL THE RESULTS BE KNOWN? Polls are scheduled to close at 8 p.m. on Monday (0200 GMT on Tuesday). Elections Alberta says it will count ballots by hand and that the question on separation will be counted first. It will publish results on the Elections Alberta website as they are received, and unofficial results are expected within 48 hours after voting ends. WHAT HAPPENS IF MOST ALBERTANS VOTE TO START THE PROCESS OF LEAVING CANADA? Smith has said she will respect the result and quickly begin the process to hold a legally binding referendum. But separation would not happen imminently. After the 1995 Quebec referendum, Canada's Parliament passed the Clarity Act in 2000, which says talks about secession can only be triggered if there is a clear majority from the public, without specifying the necessary threshold. The act also states provinces and territories have no unilateral right to leave Canada and that a constitutional amendment negotiated by provincial, territorial and federal governments is required. First Nations groups have objected to the idea of an independent Alberta, as their land treaties with Canada predate Alberta's entry into Confederation. In May, an Alberta court judge [USN:L6N41R10Y TEXT:"ruled "]the province’s chief electoral officer was wrong to allow separatists to collect signatures requesting a referendum, because the process should have prompted a consultation with Indigenous peoples whose rights might be violated by separation. Alberta has appealed the decision. WHAT HAS PRIME MINISTER MARK CARNEY SAID ABOUT THE REFERENDUM? Carney, who was largely raised in Alberta, has previously said “the best place for Alberta is in Canada” and that the country cannot succeed if it's divided. He released a video on Canadian Thanksgiving, October 12, saying national unity is critical as Canada fights threats from abroad, including a [USN:SPN44J009 TEXT:"trade war"] with the US. Carney has campaigned for Alberta to remain in Canada.

item.title: OFRBS Summary
item.description: L'Europe finit dans le rouge, pénalisée par les tensions après les événements en France
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: L'Europe finit dans le rouge, pénalisée par les tensions après les événements en France 19 octobre (Reuters) - Les Bourses européennes ont terminé en nette baisse lundi, face aux craintes d'instabilité politique et financière en France à la suite des scènes de chaos en marge de la mobilisation nationale de samedi contre la vie chère. Solvay abaisse ses objectifs annuels, le conflit au Moyen-Orient pèse 19 octobre (Reuters) - Solvay a abaissé lundi ses objectifs pour l'ensemble de l'année 2026, le groupe chimique belge prenant acte du fait que le conflit au Moyen-Orient et l'arrêt d'une usine de peroxyde en Arabie saoudite ont pesé sur ses résultats du seul troisième trimestre. Indonésie: La sécheresse provoquée par El Niño pèse sur les producteurs d’huile de palme SANGGAU, Indonésie/DJAKARTA, 19 octobre (Reuters) - Après quatre jours d'attente devant une huilerie du Kalimantan occidental, dans la partie indonésienne de Bornéo, Supendi a dû repartir avec sa récolte de fruits de palmier sur les bras, l'usine n'étant plus en mesure d'accepter de nouveaux chargements. Orange et trois opérateurs envisagent une candidature conjointe pour l'attribution de fréquences MSS FRANCFORT, 19 octobre (Reuters) - Orange, Deutsche Telekom, Telefonica et Vodafone ont annoncé lundi étudier la possibilité de présenter une offre conjointe en vue de la future attribution de fréquences pour les services mobiles par satellite (MSS) en Europe. Carrefour conclut un accord pour racheter Codifrance à Colruyt 19 octobre (Reuters) - Carrefour a annoncé lundi avoir conclu un accord avec le groupe belge Colruyt pour l’acquisition de Codifrance, spécialisé dans l’affiliation et de la distribution alimentaire de proximité, pour une valeur d'entreprise de 152 millions d'euros. Alstom remporte une commande d'environ €800 mlns au Vietnam 19 octobre (Reuters) - Alstom a annoncé lundi avoir remporté une première commande d'environ 800 millions d'euros au Vietnam pour la fourniture de trains Metropolis, à la suite d'un accord signé entre le groupe français et Vingroup. Chine-La croissance économique a accéléré plus qu'attendu au troisième trimestre PEKIN, 19 octobre (Reuters) - L'économie chinoise a accéléré au troisième trimestre à un rythme supérieur aux attentes, alors que la solidité des exportations et de l'activité manufacturière a compensé la morosité prolongée de la demande intérieure, atténuant la pression sur Pékin pour le déploiement de nouvelles mesures de stimulus afin d'atteindre l'objectif annuel de croissance. Shell s’accorde avec DCC Energy sur la cession de ses stations-service en France, selon une source Shell a scellé une entente avec DCC Energy, basée à Dublin, pour la vente de son réseau de stations-service et de services connexes en France, selon une source proche du dossier et des documents consultés par Reuters. UniCredit autorisé par la BCE à prendre le contrôle de Commerzbank UniCredit a obtenu l'autorisation de la Banque centrale européenne (BCE) pour prendre le contrôle de Commerzbank, a annoncé jeudi soir la banque italienne, alors que son offre publique d'achat hostile a porté sa participation dans son concurrent allemand à 48%. FMI: L'Europe doit stimuler la croissance ou emprunter moins pour garantir la viabilité de sa dette L'Europe doit croître plus rapidement ou emprunter moins pour maintenir sa dette sur une trajectoire viable, a déclaré vendredi le Fonds monétaire international (FMI), soulignant que les plans de redressement prévus pourraient ne pas être suffisants.

item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Yémen-Cinquante-trois morts dans une attaque houthie contre un camp militaire gouvernemental 19 octobre (Reuters) - Cinquante-trois personnes ont été tuées lundi et 200 blessées dans une attaque des rebelles houthis, soutenus par l'Iran, contre un camp d'entraînement militaire du gouvernement yéménite dans la province de Chabwa, dans l'est du Yémen, selon des responsables gouvernementaux. Italie: La police interpelle plusieurs centaines de manifestants accusés de pillage MILAN, 19 octobre (Reuters) - La police italienne a interpellé 271 individus lors des troubles survenus dimanche à Milan, ont déclaré lundi les autorités, après une deuxième journée de manifestations contre la dégradation des services publics et la hausse du coût de la vie. Grèce: Douze migrants, dont un nourrisson, se noient dans deux naufrages au large des îles grecques 19 octobre (Reuters) - Douze migrants, dont un nourrisson, se sont noyés lundi lors de deux accidents différents au large des îles grecques de Lesbos et de Samos, dans le nord-est de la mer Égée, après le chavirement de leurs embarcations alors qu'elles étaient poursuivies par les garde-côtes, ont indiqué les autorités. Australie-Une députée dans un état critique après avoir été percutée délibérement par une voiture SYDNEY, 19 octobre (Reuters) - La députée australienne Helen Haines est dans un état critique après avoir été délibérément percutée lundi par une voiture devant son bureau, à Wangaratta, au nord-est de Melbourne. Gaza-Faute de fonds, le PAM réduit son aide à 500.000 Palestiniens LE CAIRE/GAZA, 19 octobre (Reuters) - Le Programme alimentaire mondial (PAM) des Nations Unies a déclaré lundi que le manque de financement l'obligeait à réduire considérablement son programme d'aide à Gaza, laissant ainsi environ 500.000 personnes sans aide alimentaire mensuelle sur un territoire où les deux tiers de la population restent en situation d'insécurité alimentaire aiguë. La police israélienne arrête 10 personnes en lien avec les diplomates européens attaqués par des colons en Cisjordanie occupée TEl AVIV , 19 octobre (Reuters) - La police israélienne a annoncé lundi avoir arrêté dix suspects dans le cadre de son enquête sur les incidents violents survenus ce week-end en Cisjordanie occupée, notamment des agressions menées par des colons juifs à la fois contre des diplomates européens et une journaliste du Washington Post. France-Lecornu demande des couvre-feux partiels à la suite des violences PARIS, 19 octobre (Reuters) - Le Premier ministre, Sébastien Lecornu, a annoncé qu'il demandait l'instauration dès ce lundi de couvre-feux localisés et partiels en France à la suite des violences et des pillages en marge de manifestations samedi où se mêlaient revendications des lycéens et mécontentement face au coût de la vie. Brésil-Premier débat entre Bolsonaro et Lula, les attaques personnelles fusent BRASILIA, 19 octobre (Reuters) - Le sénateur Flavio Bolsonaro et le président sortant Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, qui s'affronteront lors du second tour de l'élection présidentielle au Brésil le 25 octobre, ont participé dimanche soir à un premier débat télévisé tendu lors duquel les attaques personnelles ont fusé. L'Ukraine pas avertie de nouvelles frappes russes, qui ont fait trois morts - Zelensky KYIV, 19 octobre (Reuters) - La Russie a de nouveau frappé Kyiv et ses environs sans que l'Ukraine n'ait été prévenue au préalable, a déclaré le président du pays Volodimir Zelensky, précisant que ces attaques avaient visé des infrastructures énergétiques, privant de ce fait plus de 550.000 foyers d'électricité. Canada-Un feu de prairie sur une base militaire en Alberta tue 4 personnes CALGARY, 19 octobre (Reuters) - Un incendie déclenché par un feu de broussailles a tué quatre soldats et fait 39 blessés, dont 19 se trouvent dans un état critique, sur une base d'entraînement de l'armée canadienne dans la province de l'Alberta, dans l'ouest du pays, ont déclaré dimanche soir les autorités locales.

item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Macron dit vouloir punir les "casseurs" et écouter les manifestants PARIS, 18 octobre (Reuters) - Emmanuel Macron a fait dimanche la distinction entre les "casseurs" et les manifestants aux "revendications légitimes", invitant le gouvernement à faire en sorte que le chaos constaté la veille "ne puisse pas se reproduire". Suède: La dirigeante du Parti du Centre va étudier la possibilité de former un gouvernement STOCKHOLM, 19 octobre (Reuters) - Le président du Parlement suédois a déclaré lundi avoir demandé à la dirigeante du Parti du Centre, Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist, d'étudier les possibilités de formation d'un nouveau gouvernement, lui accordant une semaine pour rencontrer les autres partis. 855 interpellations samedi à Paris, décès d'un manifestant d'un arrêt cardiorespiratoire - préfecture Un manifestant est décédé à la suite d'un arrêt cardiorespiratoire samedi à Paris lors des manifestations contre la vie chère, pendant lesquelles 855 interpellations ont été effectuées, ce qui représente un "chiffre record", a déclaré dimanche la préfecture de police. Paris condamne l'agression d'un maire français par des colons juifs La France a condamné dimanche l'agression "gravissime" par des colons juifs du maire d'Aulnoye-Aymeries survenue la veille dans le village palestinien de Taybeh. France et Allemagne d'accord sur un plan pour l'automobile La France et l'Allemagne ont annoncé vendredi un accord sur une "approche commune" visant à garantir l'avenir de l'industrie automobile européenne, avec un accent mis à la fois sur la transition énergétique et sur une production des véhicules en Europe. Les tortues caouannes, sentinelles du réchauffement en Méditerranée Sous un ciel baigné de lune, des bébés tortues sortent du sable sur la côte méditerranéenne turque et se hâtent vers la mer, dans un cycle naturel ancestral de plus en plus menacé par le changement climatique. Une étoile verte récemment découverte émerveille les astronomes Pour la première fois, des astronomes ont identifié une étoile verte, un vestige stellaire dense appelé "naine blanche", qui a pris une teinte fantomatique de vert chartreuse après avoir absorbé des débris rocheux provenant de planètes qui, autrefois, gravitaient autour d’elle. La santé du pape Léon en "amélioration constante", dit le Vatican Le pape Léon XIV continue de se remettre de son intervention chirurgicale subie mardi pour un nodule cancéreux au poumon, a déclaré vendredi le Vatican, soulignant "l'amélioration constante" de son état de santé. Le pape Léon XIV se rétablit comme prévu de son opération d'un cancer du poumon Le rétablissement du pape Léon XIV de son opération d'un cancer du poumon suit son cours, a annoncé jeudi le Vatican, qui précise que le souverain pontife de 71 ans a recommencé à travailler. Les dirigeants de l'UE se réunissent en sommet, tensions en vue sur le budget Les chefs d'Etat et de gouvernement de l'Union européenne se réunissent jeudi à Bruxelles pour un sommet lors duquel devraient être mises en exergue les divergences sur l'ampleur du prochain budget pluriannuel et sur les priorités de dépense du bloc communautaire, sans accord attendu dans l'immédiat.

item.description: Elina Svitolina annonce se séparer de Gaël Monfils, invoquant les conséquences de la guerre
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Elina Svitolina annonce se séparer de Gaël Monfils, invoquant les conséquences de la guerre 19 octobre (Reuters) - Elina Svitolina, sixième joueuse mondiale de tennis, a annoncé lundi se séparer du Français Gaël Monfils, ancien numéro six mondial du circuit ATP, l'Ukrainienne précisant que le poids émotionnel de la guerre menée par la Russie contre son pays natal l'avait amenée à ressentir le besoin de se redécouvrir. Voile-Barrier, première femme en solitaire sur un géant des mers Alexia Barrier paraît toute petite à la barre d'Idec Sport-CIC, un trimaran de 32 mètres capable de filer à plus de 40 nœuds. Bientôt, elle sera seule à bord. Cyclisme-Seixas remporte le Tour de Lombardie, son premier monument Paul Seixas (Decathlon-CMA CGM) a remporté samedi le premier monument du cyclisme de sa jeune carrière en triomphant sur le Tour de Lombardie, dont il est devenu le plus jeune vainqueur de l'histoire devant l'Espagnol Enric Mas (Movistar) et l'Italien Giulio Ciccone (Lidl-Trek). Basket-Wembanyama soutient les manifestations lycéennes La star du basket français Victor Wembanyama a apporté jeudi soir son soutien aux lycéens et étudiants qui manifestent depuis plusieurs semaines pour exiger de meilleures conditions d'enseignement. Football: Ceferin finalement candidat à sa réélection à la tête de l'UEFA Le président de l'UEFA Aleksander Ceferin a annoncé jeudi qu'il était finalement candidat à sa réélection à la tête de l'instance européenne. Football: Infantino réaffirme le soutien de la Fifa au football africain Le président de la Fifa, Gianni Infantino, a promis jeudi davantage de moyens pour l'Afrique lors d'une conférence au Cap-Vert dans l'un de ses rares discours publics depuis son projet avorté de céder une partie des droits commerciaux des compétitions de la Fifa à des investisseurs privés. Rallye: Les organisateurs du Dakar envisagent un autre parcours en Arabie saoudite Les organisateurs du Dakar travaillent sur un parcours alternatif pour que la 49e édition, prévue en janvier, puisse se tenir en Arabie saoudite malgré la situation au Moyen-Orient, ont indiqué à Reuters trois sources impliquées dans le championnat du monde de rallye-raid . Basket: La NBA et la Fiba réaffirment leur volonté de lancer une ligue européenne La NBA et la Fédération internationale de basket (Fiba) ont réaffirmé jeudi leur intention de créer une ligue en Europe, deux jours après le rejet par l'Euroligue d'une proposition de collaboration formulée par son homologue nord-américaine, qui souhaite lancer son projet NBA Europe à l'automne 2027. Football: Arsenal prolonge son entraîneur Mikel Arteta jusqu'en 2030 Arsenal a annoncé mercredi la prolongation de contrat de son entraîneur Mikel Arteta jusqu'en 2030 après une saison remarquable lors de laquelle il a mené le club londonien au titre de Premier League et en finale de la Ligue des champions. Football-Messi fait ses adieux à l'équipe d'Argentine Lionel Messi a signé mardi une dernière prestation de grande classe, marquant un but et délivrant deux passes décisives à l'occasion de son ultime match sous le maillot de l'équipe d'Argentine remporté face au Bénin (3-0), en amical, après une carrière internationale de 21 ans.
